Hi T.J.,

Thanks for the photo, it tells me a lot. Your board is on the network (phone hidden), wifi connected), the BM1370 side is detected, the temperature is a cold 32 C and the power reads 0.062 W with 0.0 GH/s. That means the miner is powering up fine but the firmware is cutting the ASIC core rail straight away and showing the protection screen, so it never gets to hash. A reboot will not clear that on its own, which matches what you are seeing.

On the code itself I want to be straight with you: #···· is not documented in the firmware release notes or the public issue tracker, and I will not guess at it. I have passed it to JD, our hardware lead, with your photo and the readings. Other codes in that family point either at the 12V input or at the voltage regulator, and the checks below are what separate the two.

The first thing to test is the power supply, because it is the most common cause by far and the stock bricks are often marginal. Could you tell me which supply you are using and what it is rated for (volts and amps, printed on the label), and if you have a second 12V supply with enough current, try the unit on that one. While the unit is unplugged, also give the yellow blade fuse and the XT60 pigtail a look: a fuse that has popped or a connector that has been warmed up is worth knowing about before anything else.

Second, firmware. Open http://192.168.2.212 in a browser on the same network and tell me the version it reports. Compare it with the current version shown in the flasher at harlolabs.com, and if you are behind, do a full factory flash (erase, then install, not an over the air update) with a USB data cable. A partial or corrupted image can throw a protection trip like this, so a clean install is worth doing even if the version looks right.

Last, if you can, send a short video from plugging it in until the error appears, plus a clear photo of the serial number label. With the supply ruled out and a clean flash still giving the same screen, that is what settles it as a board level fault rather than anything in software.

One safety note: if you ever smell burning, see smoke or find the plug hot, unplug it at the wall and stop there, do not keep rebooting it.

The team picks this up tomorrow at 10am ET and JD's read on that code comes back to you in this thread. If you want a faster answer tonight, the Harlo Discord is very active: https://discord.gg/Q2R5sA9Fsf , mention @nullhashrate (that is JD) and post the same photo.

Hal, HeliumDeploy technical support

I’m running a 350 Meanwell PSU. I tried another one with the same issue so
it’s not the PSU.

I’ll try to flash the FW and try again. I’ll repot back tomorrow.

Thanks,
T.J. S.

Hi T.J.,

Good, that is the most useful thing you could have told me. A Meanwell 350 is plenty of supply, and a second one behaving the same way takes the power source off the list, so whatever is cutting the core rail is on the board or in the firmware.

For the flash, use the flasher at harlolabs.com in Chrome or Edge, pick the NerdQaxe++ profile, and do the factory image with a full erase rather than the over the air update. The factory route writes from the start of flash and wipes saved settings, which is exactly what you want here, since a half written image or a stored frequency and voltage pair from an earlier session can both produce a protection trip. Use a USB data cable straight to the board's port, not a charge only cable, and leave the 12V off while it flashes.

When it comes back up, leave it on the default frequency and voltage for the first run and let it sit for ten minutes before you change anything. If it hashes at stock, the settings were the problem and we can walk the clocks back up slowly. If the protection screen returns, go to http://192.168.2.212 in a browser, note the firmware version it reports, and grab the log page there if you can, that log shows the exact moment the ASIC voltage is set and then forced back to zero, which is the line that tells us whether the regulator is tripping or the input is sagging.

Along with that, a short video from power on until the error appears and a clear photo of the serial number label would let me close this out properly. Please do not open the supply or touch anything on the mains side, and if you ever smell burning or see smoke, unplug at the wall and stop.

JD, our hardware lead, has your photo and that #···· code and picks it up tomorrow at 10am ET, and his read comes back to you in this thread. If you want a faster answer in the meantime, the Harlo Discord is very active at https://discord.gg/Q2R5sA9Fsf , mention @nullhashrate and post the same photo.

Hal, HeliumDeploy technical support

Searched the web · nerdqaxe++ rev 6.1 firmware image same as rev6 flasher profi

Hi T.J.,

Yes, I opened your screenshot: the list shows NERDOCTAXE REV3, NERDQAXE REV5, NERDQAXE REV6 (highlighted), NerdQaxe++ Rev.7 and NEXUS L1. For a Rev 6.1 unit the right entry is NERDQAXE REV6. There is no separate 6.1 image, because 6.1 is a small spin of the rev6 board and it runs the same profile.

Please do not pick NerdQaxe++ Rev.7. Rev7 is a different board with a different power stage (the upstream project lists rev7 separately as the TPS546 board, which is why it has its own entry), and a rev7 image on a rev6 board can set the core rail up wrongly, which is the last thing we want on a unit that is already tripping voltage protection.

Worth confirming the revision before you write anything, since you are flashing on top of a fault. Open http://192.168.2.212 while the old firmware is still on there and look at the board version it reports on the system or settings page. 501 is the Rev 6.1 board and 502 is rev7. If it says 501, take REV6 and go ahead. If it says something else, send me the number and the version string and I will tell you which entry matches before you flash.

Then do the erase and install, not the over the air path, leave the 12V off during the flash, and use a USB data cable. When it comes back up, leave frequency and voltage at the defaults and let it run ten minutes before changing anything. If it hashes, we tune up slowly from there. If the protection screen comes back on a clean Harlo OS install at stock settings, tell me the exact text it shows now, the firmware version, and send a short video from power on to the error plus a photo of the serial label. That combination is what settles whether this is the regulator on the board.

JD still has your original screen and the #···· code and picks it up tomorrow at 10am ET, with his answer coming back in this thread. For a faster read tonight, the Harlo Discord is at https://discord.gg/Q2R5sA9Fsf , mention @nullhashrate.

Hal, HeliumDeploy technical support

Hi T.J.,

That is the unit coming back to life. I opened both screenshots. The log line that matters is the pair: "NerdQaxe++ Rev6.1 controller map matched; ASIC rails are off" and then, a fraction of a second later, "ASIC rails enabled at 1150 mV per domain", followed by BM1370 chips 1, 2, 3 and 4 detected and a chip count of 4. On the old firmware the rails were being cut and never came back, which is what put the protection screen up. Now they come up and stay up, and all four chips enumerate. So this was firmware, not the board and not your Meanwell.

A few things on the dashboard so you know what is normal. The 15.2 TH/s is a very short window estimate taken seconds after start, and with the ASIC at 21.5 C and the VR at 26.6 C the chips have barely warmed up yet. Give it twenty to thirty minutes and the figure will settle toward the unit's real average, around 5 to 6 TH/s at stock settings, with ASIC temperatures climbing into the normal running range. Judge it on the settled number and on accepted shares, not on the first reading.

"No device power reading" is expected rather than a fault. Harlo OS deliberately does not let the miner estimate its own wattage, it reads power from a smart plug at the wall, so until you pair one that field stays blank. Hash still comes from the shares your pool accepts, so the dashboard is telling you the truth about the mining side.

One thing to look at: the log shows pool 2 authorizing, which means it fell back to your secondary. Open the pool settings and check the primary entry, the stratum URL, the port and the worker name, since best share is still 0 and it will stay 0 until shares are being accepted and one of them is large enough to record. The two gpio conflict warnings on GPIO 1 and 13 are warnings at boot, not errors, and the boot carried on normally through chip detection, so I would not chase them.

Let it mine overnight at stock and tell me tomorrow what the hashrate averages and what the ASIC and VR temperatures settle at, and whether shares are landing on your primary pool. If the protection screen ever returns, send me the log around it and we pick straight up from there.

Hal, HeliumDeploy technical support

Hi T.J.,

Thanks for going all the way through that, including the full esptool wipe. I opened the new log and it is the clearest evidence we have had.

Two lines tell the story. The regulator reports TPS536X7_status with word 8841 and vout 10, which is a latched undervoltage fault on the core output with power good dropped and the converter switched off, and the input status is clean at 00. The line underneath confirms it from the other side: vin 12.06 V, so your Meanwell is delivering exactly what it should, but vout 0.00, iout 0.00 and pout 0.00, with the regulator sitting cold at 19.75 C and the board at 29.62 C. Good 12V going in, nothing coming out, and no heat or load anywhere, so this is not thermal, not the supply, and not the chips pulling it down.

Put that next to everything we have already eliminated. Two power supplies, one of them a 350 W Meanwell. Two completely different firmwares, Harlo OS and stock NerdQAxe OS. A full chip erase between them, so no leftover settings or half written image. The brief run where all four BM1370 enumerated and it still never produced a share fits the same picture, a core rail that comes up weakly or not at all and then latches off. That points at the core voltage regulator on the board itself rather than anything you can fix from the software side, and nothing further you do at home will change that reading.

So please stop power cycling it and leave it unplugged for now, there is nothing left to test and no reason to keep stressing the regulator.

I have written up my findings, the log lines and everything we tried, and passed them to the team. They pick this up today at 10am ET and you will get their answer in this thread. One thing that will save a round trip: if you can reply with a clear photo of the serial number label on the board, it will be sitting there waiting for them.

Hal, HeliumDeploy technical support

Hi T.J.,

No problem, that sticker goes missing often enough and it does not hold anything up. We can identify the unit other ways.

If the board is still powered up and reachable, the easiest substitute is the network identity the firmware reports. Open the web UI and note the MAC address and the hostname it shows, plus the firmware version and the board version it reports (501 for your Rev 6.1). Those three together pin the board down. If you would rather not power it again, a plain photo of the back of the board showing the empty sticker area and any numbers printed in the silkscreen works too, and your order reference already ties it to the right unit on our side.

Everything else is already in the file: the original protection screen, the TPS536X7 status word with the latched undervoltage on the core rail, the 12.06 V in against 0.00 V out, and the fact that it survived two supplies, two firmwares and a full erase.

The team is reviewing the return now and will confirm by email shortly, in this same thread. Until then leave the unit unplugged, there is nothing more to test on it.

Hal, HeliumDeploy technical support
